title: Resveratrol reduces obesity in high-fat diet-fed mice via modulating the composition and metabolic function of the gut microbiota - ScienceDirect
abstract:

Resveratrol (RSV) is a natural polyphenol with anti-obesity effects. However, the mechanisms of anti-obesity remain unclear due to its low bioavailability. Recent evidence demonstrates that gut microbiota plays a key role in obesity. This spurred us to investigate whether the anti-obesity effects of RSV are related to modulations in the gut microbiota and metabolic functions.
The keywords used include “polyphenols”, “gut microbiota”, “short-chain fatty acids”, “bile acids”, “trimethylamine N-oxide”, “lipopolysaccharides” “tryptophan”, “dopamine”, “intestinal barrier”, “central nervous system”, “lung”, “anthocyanin”, “proanthocyanidin”, “baicalein”, “caffeic acid”, “curcumin”, “epigallocatechin-3-gallate”, “ferulic acid”, “genistein”, “kaempferol”, “luteolin”, “myricetin”, “naringenin”, “procyanidins”, “protocatechuic acid”, “pterostilbene”, “quercetin”, “resveratrol”, etc. The review first demonstrates that polyphenols significantly alter gut microbiota diversity (α- and β-diversity) and the abundance of specific microorganisms.
The main goal of this study was to identify the mechanism by which RSV and gut microbiota interacts to affect HFD-induced obesity. The results showed that RSV supplementation improved metabolic phenotype, ameliorated intestinal oxidative stress, modulated the gut microbiota composition and function in HFD mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation from RSV to HFD mice was able to reverse weight gain and improve gut microbiota composition and intestinal permeability. Moreover, metabolomic analyses combined with antibiotic experiments verified 3-HPP and 4-HPA were the two gut metabolites of RSV.
Globally, obesity and its associated metabolic diseases have spread dramatically throughout developed and developing countries [1]. Obesity is caused by numerous factors, including host genetics, physiological characteristics, living environment and lifestyle [2,3]. Intriguingly, growing evidence supports that gut microbiota is associated with energy balance, glucose metabolism, insulin resistance and oxidative stress [4].
